_meta.description: The record of what the piece does not say, and why. Rendered to the reader as a section of the publication, not held internally. If a claim here reappears in a draft, it reappears in error.

cuts.claim: A quotation attributed to Beaty (1969) on investigations blaming the pilot unless something was found wrong with the aircraft.
cuts.reason: Not traced to a page in either edition. The wording circulates in secondary retellings. A paraphrase of an unlocatable quotation is a fabrication with the evidence removed.

cuts.claim: Helmreich et al. (1990) on the effectiveness question remaining open.
cuts.reason: RESCUED. The Flight Safety Digest issue is open-access and the wording is in the freely available text.

cuts.claim: That Kegworth is credited with re-modelling CRM from Cockpit to Crew resource management.
cuts.reason: No RAeS or UK CAA source found asserting it. Chronologically impossible as an origin claim: the rename sits in the US second generation around 1986, and Kegworth is January 1989.
searched: FAA and RAeS copies of the CRM history paper

cuts.claim: That US manufacturer assistance in the 1990s drove Chinese CRM adoption.
cuts.reason: Not found in any primary CAAC source across two search rounds. Also sits close to the pattern the piece's own red team warns about: treating US influence as the engine of non-US adoption because US sources are the ones written in English.

cuts.claim: Indonesian causal linkages resting on material described in the briefs as AI-generated.
cuts.reason: Categorically disqualified rather than weakly sourced. Generated material has no author who observed anything. The external round re-sourced the surrounding facts: the EU blanket ban via Commission Regulation 787/2007 and the FAA IASA Category 2 downgrade are both primary and documented.

cuts.claim: Aeroflot's reported internal CRM standard of roughly thirty academic hours over three years.
cuts.reason: Sourced only to Russian-language blogs and aggregators. Failed to verify across three rounds against Rosaviatsiya federal aviation rules or Aeroflot documentation.

cuts.claim: Nine quotation fragments across four sources in the union-resistance and leak sections, with no document-level attribution.
cuts.reason: PARTIALLY RESCUED. The union position is now attributable to specific published items, and the safety-agency response to the leak is attributable to named outlets. The regulator's privacy statement is traced to correspondence but no standalone document URL was isolated.

cuts.claim: Two phrases quoted from the Paris Court of Appeal judgment of 21 May 2026.
cuts.reason: The conviction, the maximum corporate fine, and the pending appeal to the Cour de cassation are all confirmed. One quoted phrase corresponds to a French formulation carried by a news agency; the other was not located. Retain the procedural facts, cut the unlocated phrase.

cuts.claim: That an aviation-specific methodological critique of applying national culture dimensions to cockpit behaviour exists.
cuts.reason: Searched across two rounds and not located. The general ecological-fallacy critique is robust and peer-reviewed but is not aviation-specific. The near-absence is itself reportable and should be stated rather than papered over with the general literature.

cuts.claim: That the aviation insurance industry drove CRM adoption.
cuts.reason: No evidence found. The canonical histories trace every driver and never mention insurers. Where insurers discuss CRM they treat it as a cause of improved loss experience, which reverses the direction of causation. The union role is documented; the manufacturer role is weak and later. This absence is a finding and must be stated openly, because leaving it silent would tilt the causal account toward the institutional explanation by default.
